Spotted wolffish (Anarhichas minor) hatch from demersal, yolk-laden eggs following an incubation period of approximately 300 days [ab = approximately 300 days] at 3.5 °C [T = 3.5 °C]. Emerging yolk-sac larvae measure approximately 2.25 centimeters [Lb = approximately 2.25 centimeters] in total length at birth, a size that equips them for the extended endotrophic phase typical of this cold-water species. The onset of exogenous feeding follows yolk-sac resorption, and the pelagic larval phase proceeds under the influence of ambient temperatures, with growth rates closely tied to thermal conditions. Comparative studies among anarhichadids indicate that the spotted wolffish exhibits a slightly faster larval development than the closely related Atlantic wolffish, though both share a prolonged embryonic period relative to most boreal teleosts. The encapsulated eggs are deposited in dense clusters, often guarded by the male until hatching, a reproductive behavior that likely reduces egg mortality in the harsh benthic environment.

Field surveys and captive rearing studies have allowed researchers to estimate the maximum attainable size of this species. Spotted wolffish can reach a total length of up to 180 centimeters [Li = up to 180 centimeters] in their natural deep-water habitats along the continental slopes of the North Atlantic. This ultimate total length, corresponding to an asymptotic body size, is among the largest recorded for any member of the family Anarhichadidae. In terms of body mass, the ultimate wet weight of a fully grown individual approaches 27,900 grams [Wwi = 27,900 grams]. Such a substantial mass reflects the slow, sustained growth trajectory and the lipid-rich diet of benthic invertebrates and echinoderms that characterizes the species throughout its long life. The large body size also confers advantages in both predator avoidance and competitive dominance for nesting sites on the rocky seafloor.

The transition to reproductive maturity in spotted wolffish occurs after several years of steady growth, with females typically attaining first reproduction between 6 and 8 years of age. Data from long-term tagging studies indicate that the age at first reproduction, recorded at a stable temperature of 3.5 °C [T = 3.5 °C], is approximately 7 years after hatching [tR = approximately 7 years after hatching]. At this life stage, individuals have typically reached a length at puberty of roughly 55 centimeters [Lp = roughly 55 centimeters] total length, with estimates ranging from 50 to 60 centimeters depending on local environmental conditions and food availability. The corresponding wet weight at puberty has been calculated at about 796 grams [Wwp = about 796 grams], a mass that represents a significant energetic investment prior to the initiation of gonadal recrudescence. This comparatively late maturation is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes somatic growth and the accumulation of lipid reserves before reproduction commences.

Reproductive output in spotted wolffish is characterized by a high fecundity coupled with a relatively low annual spawning frequency. Females produce large batches of adhesive demersal eggs, with an estimated fecundity of approximately 35,200 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 35,200 eggs per clutch] based on direct counts from gravid individuals. However, the frequency of reproduction is low, with spawning occurring only once every ten years; available data indicate that females produce approximately 0.1 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 0.1 clutches per year], a rate that reflects the high energetic cost of vitellogenesis in cold waters. The maximum lifespan of the species, observed under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 3.5 °C [T = 3.5 °C], extends to about 21 years [am = about 21 years], though individuals in the wild may experience somewhat shorter lives due to natural mortality factors such as predation and fishing pressure.

The early life stages of spotted wolffish are characterized by a prolonged period of yolk dependence, during which the developing larvae rely entirely on endogenous reserves. Based on the diameter of freshly spawned eggs, which averages approximately 5.5 millimeters, the calculated wet weight at birth is 0.087 grams [Wwb = 0.087 grams]. This modest initial mass belies the substantial yolk volume that sustains the alevin through an extended lecithotrophic phase at 3.5 °C [T = 3.5 °C]. The relatively large egg size compared to many other perciform fishes ensures that hatchlings emerge at a well-developed stage, likely reducing mortality during the vulnerable transition to exogenous feeding. Comparative physiological research on congeneric species indicates that the metabolic rate of spotted wolffish larvae is finely tuned to the cold, stable temperatures of their boreal habitat, with optimal growth and survival observed consistently at the aforementioned thermal regime.
